notes.text: We have here the general establishment of God's covenant with this new world, and the extent of that covenant.

There shall not any more be a flood — God had drowned the world once, and still it is as provoking as ever; yet he will never drown it any more, for he deals not with us according to our sins. This promise of God keeps the sea and clouds in their decreed place, and sets them gates and bars, Hitherto they shall come, Job xxxviii, 10, 11. If the sea should flow but for a few days, as it doth twice every day for a few hours, what desolations would it make? So would the clouds, if such showers as we have sometimes seen, were continued long. But God by flowing seas, and sweeping rains, shews what he could do in wrath; and yet by preserving the earth from being deluged between both, shews what he can do in mercy, and will do in truth.

I set my bow in the clouds — The rainbow, 'tis likely was seen in the clouds before, but was never a seal of the covenant 'till now. Now, concerning this seal of the covenant, observe, (1.) This seal is affixed with repeated assurances of the truth of that promise, which it was designed to be the ratification of; I do set my bow in the cloud, ver. 13. It shall be seen in the cloud, ver. 14. and it shall be a token of the covenant, ver. 12, 13. And I will remember my covenant, that the waters shall no more become a flood, ver. 15. Nay, as if the eternal Mind needed a memorandum, I will look upon it that I may remember the everlasting covenant, ver. 16. (2.) The rainbow appears when the clouds are most disposed to wet; when we have most reason to fear the rain prevailing, God shews this seal of the promise that it shall not prevail. (3.) The rainbow appears when one part of the sky is clear, which imitates mercy remembered in the midst of wrath, and the clouds are hemmed as it were with the rainbow, that it may not overspread the heavens, for the bow is coloured rain, or the edges of a cloud gilded. As God looks upon the bow that he may remember the covenant, so should we, that we also may be ever mindful of the covenant with faith and thankfulness.

glossa.text: « Flesh with blood. » ((ISID.)) All animals are given them for food, because in the calling of the Gentiles to the faith there is no difference, which is figured in the dish of Peter. They are forbidden to eat blood, lest the former life be held as it were stifled within the conscience, but let it be poured out through confession. The eating of flesh seems to have been granted after the flood, on account of the barrenness of the earth and the frailty of man.

« Behold, I will establish my compact, » etc. God set a testament between himself and men and every living soul, that he might not destroy it by a flood, the bow, namely, which appears in the clouds, which never shines save from the sun. For those perish not in the flood, separated from the Church, who in the prophets and in all the holy Scriptures, as in the clouds of God, acknowledge the glory of Christ and seek not their own. But lest the worshippers of this sun swell up, let them know that Christ is signified by the sun just as by the lion, by the lamb, by the stone, for the sake of likeness, not by any substance of property.

« I will set my bow, » etc. ((ALC. in Gen.)) God gave the bow for a sign of security, lest fearful men should dread to be destroyed by another flood, often beholding the overflowing of the rains. This is set in the heaven, that it may be seen by all, and that in whatever tribulation we may lift up to him the eyes of our heart who dwells in the heavens. But because the bow is not save from the rays of the sun and a moist cloud, it seems that before the flood there had been no rains. The earth, however, could be made fruitful from dew and from the overflowing of the springs.

((STRAB.)) The bow has two colours, blue and fiery, which express two judgments: one of water, which is past; the other of fire, which is believed to be to come at the end of the world: whence the blue colour is on the outside, but the fiery within.

notes.text: Cause — Without any provocation of mine.
Teach — Teach me my duty, and cause me to keep close to it, notwithstanding all temptations.
Upright — Holy and true, in all his declarations and offers of mercy to sinners. Therefore - He will not be wanting to such poor sinners as I am, but will guide them into the way of life and peace.
The meek — Such as meekly submit themselves to God, and are desirous to be directed and governed by him. Judgment - In the paths of judgment, in the right way.
Paths — All the dealings of God with them, yea even those that are afflictive, are done in kindness and faithfulness to them.

glossa.text:
*Unto the end.* ((Hier.)) Here the penitent who has been scourged is set before the rest, lest they murmur in adversities: he who, having had the trial in himself, coaxes through mercy and terrifies through justice.

 *To thee, O Lord, have I lifted up.* ((AUG.)) A psalm against the adversities of the world, etc., *as far as* who not through all, the less perfect.

((CASS.)) First he asks to be taught the ways of the Lord, because he is raised up toward God.

((ID.)) Toward the contemplating of thee; he easily despises earthly things who beholds things divine.

*I trust.* ((ID.)) Having had trial of my own weakness in evils, I shall not blush because of my enemies.

*Neither let my enemies laugh at me:* and I am sure that he deceives none that endures patiently.

*In vain.* ((ID.)) Because all things are vain and unfruitful which are alien from God.

*Shew me thy ways, O Lord.* ((CASS.)) The ways are of the order of life, etc., *as far as: Direct,* belongs to life, *teach* to knowledge.

*Teach.* ((AUG.)) Truth itself, that I may understand what I believe, because I have endured; and if this suffices not: *Remember.*

*God my saviour.* ((CASS.)) There are two things which make men good, that we believe God our saviour, and that we patiently await his retribution.

*Remember.* ((ID.)) Of former sins and of those which are daily done, he prays through the mercy shewn to the ancients, and because he fears a true judge.

*Of thy tender mercies.* Compassion is properly in the shewing forth of good things.

*Which are from of old.* ((AUG.)) That is, they are from the beginning of the world: therefore let him not fail in me.

*Sins.* ((CASS.)) They are when the way of equity is forsaken.

*Of my youth.* Not for age, but for the rashness of headlong haste, which is then, when the heat of the mind exceeds moderation.

*Ignorances.* We do those things which we do not know to be evil. Or the sins of ignorance in little ones, who are held at any rate by original sin.

((HIER.)) Of my youth. Before I went out of the house of my wicked father.

*Remember me, thou.* ((AUG.)) Whose work it is to have mercy and to forgive sins.

*According to thy mercy.* That is, thy mercy is ample. Mercy is toward the wretched, goodness toward any whatsoever. But God does good both when implored by the wretched, and when led by his goodness: none is good but God.

*Sweet.* ((ID.)) Because he forgives all former things, where grace is without merits.

*Right.* Because after mercy, etc., *as far as Sweet,* because he gives sweet things; *right,* because he corrects.

*Therefore.* ((CASS.)) Because he is sweet and right; not out of cruelty, but out of kindness.

*In the way.* That is, faith, or the precepts of God. Or in the way of this life, where one must live rightly, he will give a law.

*In judgment.* While he punishes, he will direct to better things. But let them be meek who are corrected: for from wild beasts they are tamed, that they may bear it. For if they are mild, that is, of a gentle mind, as though having this by nature: he will teach them the precepts for the neglect of which came the scourges.

*Mercy and truth.* ((AUG.)) But what ways he will teach, etc., *as far as* and then he guards against the severity of the judge.

*Testament.* ((CASS.)) The New, which is excellently called a Testament, where there is a clear and certain promise of an inheritance, which is confirmed by death also.

*And the Testament.* Of the old law, where the Prophets were witnesses of the promises.

notes.text: For — This is undoubtedly best, whereby we are most conformed to Christ. Now Christ suffered once - To suffer no more. For sins - Not his own, but ours. The just for the unjust - The word signifies, not only them who have wronged their neighbours, but those who have transgressed any of the commands of God; as the preceding word, just, denotes a person who has fulfilled, not barely social duties, but all kind of righteousness. That he might bring us to God - Now to his gracious favour, hereafter to his blissful presence, by the same steps of suffering and of glory. Being put to death in the flesh - As man. But raised to life by the Spirit - Both by his own divine power, and by the power of the Holy Ghost.

By which Spirit he preached — Through the ministry of Noah. To the spirits in prison - The unholy men before the flood, who were then reserved by the justice of God, as in a prison, till he executed the sentence upon them all; and are now also reserved to the judgment of the great day.
When the longsuffering of God waited — For an hundred and twenty years; all the time the ark was preparing: during which Noah warned them all to flee from the wrath to come.

The antitype whereof — The thing typified by the ark, even baptism, now saveth us - That is, through the water of baptism we are saved from the sin which overwhelms the world as a flood: not, indeed, the bare outward sign, but the inward grace; a divine consciousness that both our persons and our actions are accepted through him who died and rose again for us.
Angels and authorities and powers — That is, all orders both of angels and men.

glossa.text: *He might offer to God. ((ID.))* Because even then, if any had been willing to believe at the preaching of the Lord (which they set forth through the life of the faithful), he rejoiced to offer them to God the Father. But if any disparaged the good as though they were evildoers, at the imminence of the flood they were confounded.

*In prison. ((ID.))* They who have their sense darkened with shadows are rightly said to be shut up in prison even in this life, and in this inward prison of the mind they are weighed down by unjust works, until, loosed from the flesh, they are cast into the exterior darkness of eternal damnation. The just also have a prison here, but one of tribulations, whereas the reprobate have one of vices.

*When they waited for the patience of God.* When the patience of God invited them to repentance, sparing them for the hundred years in which Noe was building the ark, by which was shown what was to come to pass in the world. They therefore did not use the patience of God unto repentance, but awaited it as though it were going to endure for ever. *Noe.* Noe is interpreted rest, and signifies Christ who gives to his faithful the rest of souls.

*When the ark was a building. ((BEDA.))* As the ark was built of planed timbers, so the Church of the gathering of faithful souls: and as, when the world was perishing, few were saved by water: so, in comparison with those that perish, small is the number of the elect, because narrow is the way which leads to life, and few there are that find it.

*Whereunto you also of the like form.* Baptism makes men safe, baptism, I say, *of the like form,* that is, likened in all things to that ark, because whatsoever is there done carnally, here is done spiritually.

*Not the putting away of the flesh,* etc. I do not say that that baptism saves where there is only *a putting away of the filth of the flesh,* that is, where the flesh only is washed outwardly (which the heretics had), but where there is *the examination of a pure conscience,* that is, where a good conscience of him that is to be baptized is asked and required by the baptizer: because such a baptism saves, another kills; the examination has been made tending unto God, that through a good conscience he may be made one with God.

*Swallowing up death. ((BEDA.))* What we swallow down, we bring it about that, taken into our bodies, it nowhere appears: so the Lord utterly consumed death, that it might avail nothing against him, and, the appearance of a true body remaining, the stain of the ancient frailty was absent. Which is promised to us also, whence he adds, *that we also might be made heirs of eternal life. The angels being made subject to him.* We do not doubt that the angels were always subject to the Son of God, but he here makes mention of the subjection for this reason, that he might show the assumed humanity so exalted in the resurrection that it is preferred before every power of angelic dignity. Whence, *thou hast subjected all things under his feet ((Psal. VIII))*.

notes.text: And immediately the Spirit thrusteth him out into the wilderness — So in all the children of God, extraordinary manifestations of his favour are wont to be followed by extraordinary temptations. Matt. iv, 1; Luke iv, 1.

And he was there forty days, tempted by Satan — Invisibly. After this followed the temptation by him in a visible shape, related by St. Matthew. And he was with the wild beasts - Though they had no power to hurt him. St. Mark not only gives us a compendium of St. Matthew's Gospel, but likewise several valuable particulars, which the other evangelists have omitted.
The time is fulfilled — The time of my kingdom, foretold by Daniel, expected by you, is fully come.

glossa.text:
*And he was baptized in the Jordan.* For three causes: that he might fulfil justice and humility; that he might approve the baptism of John; that, sanctifying the waters of Jordan by the descent of the dove, he might show the Holy Ghost to be present in baptism.

((HIER.)) Mark: As the hart, longing for the fountains of waters, gives leaps, crops the tops of the meadows, bears palms upon his crown, so, like the honey-flowing bee, he tastes but lightly the flowers of the field (to which the odour of the true Isaac is likened). Whence Jesus coming from Nazareth of Galilee to the baptism, etc., *as far as: To him that overcometh I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God ((Apoc. II))*.

*He saw the heavens opened,* etc. ((BEDA.)) The mystery of the Trinity is shown in the baptism: the Son is baptized, the Spirit is in the dove, the Father sounds in the voice. The heavens are opened, etc., *as far as* the Spirit shall abide with us and shall be in us according to the measure of faith. But of Christ it is said: *Full of grace and truth ((Joan. I))*.

*Remaining in him.* The Spirit remains in him, not from the time he was baptized, but from the time he was conceived. But that he descended at the baptism signifies that spiritual grace is given to us in baptism, to whom, being regenerated of water and the Spirit unto the remission of sins, a fuller grace of the Spirit is wont to be given from heaven by the imposition of the bishop's hand.

*Thou art my beloved Son. ((BEDA.))* He is not taught what he knew not, but it is shown to us what we ought to believe, namely that he, etc., *as far as* and rightly did the Spirit descend in the likeness of a dove, which is a simple creature and without gall: because he seeks the simple, nor does he dwell in impure minds.

*The Spirit. ((ID.))* Lest it be doubtful which spirit, Luke deliberately sets before it: *Jesus being full of the Holy Ghost returned from the Jordan;* then he added: *and was led by the Spirit into the desert, lest an unclean* spirit be thought to have had any power against him.

*Forty days. ((ID.))* It signifies the whole time in which the devil tempts his members. For the fourfold world, by the observance of the ten commandments, serves the Lord in striving against the devil. And four times ten make forty. Everywhere and always the adversary is at hand, who ceases not to hinder our journey.

*And he was with the beasts.* We also, if in the desert of holy conversation we bear with undefiled mind the bestial manners of men, deserve the mystery of the angels, by whom, loosed from the body, we may be carried over into heaven

*But after that. ((ISID.))* We have received grace for grace, things carnal are beheaded, things spiritual are quickened. The shadow ceasing, the truth is at hand. John in prison, the law in Judaea, Jesus in Galilee, salvation among the Gentiles.

*Preaching,* etc. *((HIER.)) Blessed are the poor in spirit, for they shall possess ((Matth. V))*, etc. To the earthly kingdom succeeds poverty, and to the poverty of Christians an everlasting kingdom; whence: *My kingdom is not of this world ((Joan. XVIII))*: for every earthly honour is froth, smoke, a dream.

*Repent ye. ((HIER.))* The sweetness of the fruit makes up for the bitterness of the root: the hope of the harbour delights away the perils of the sea, the hope of health softens the pain of the medicine. He who desires the kernel, let him break the nut: let him do penance who wishes to cleave to the eternal good. They can tell forth the praises of Christ who have deserved to come to the palm of pardon. Whence after penance preachers are chosen.

Prepare the way of the Lord

Lord, who throughout these forty days

echoes.text: When men began to multiply on the surface of the ground, and daughters were born to them, God’s sons saw that men’s daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives. Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.” The Nephilim were in the earth in those days, and also after that, when God’s sons came in to men’s daughters and had children […]
echoes.note: The flood narrative is invoked typologically: 'the days of Noah while the ship was being built' (3:20). Peter reads the wickedness and judgment of the antediluvian world (Gen 6) as the backdrop against which the ark/baptism deliverance is the antitype (antitypos, 3:21). The flood's saving-through-water becomes the type fulfilled in baptism — explicitly figural.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Noah, “Come with all of your household into the ship, for I have seen your righteousness before me in this generation. You shall take seven pairs of every clean animal with you, the male and his female. Of the animals that are not clean, take two, the male and his female. Also of the birds of the sky, seven and seven, male and female, to keep seed alive on the surface of all the earth. In seven days, I will cause it to rain on the earth for […]
echoes.note: 'Few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water' (3:20) cites the ark deliverance of Genesis 7 (Noah, his wife, three sons and their wives = eight). The salvation 'through water' is the explicit antitype of baptism in 3:21 — the flood-water that destroyed the disobedient world saves the elect remnant in the ark. Typological/figural reading of the flood as baptism.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: 'Who is at the right hand of God' (3:22) cites the enthronement formula of Psalm 110:1 'Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.' The subjection of 'angels and authorities and powers' to the exalted Christ realizes the footstool-of-enemies motif. The most-cited royal psalm for Christ's exaltation.

echoes.text: God remembered Noah, all the animals, and all the livestock that were with him in the ship; and God made a wind to pass over the earth. The waters subsided. The deep’s fountains and the sky’s windows were also stopped, and the rain from the sky was restrained. The waters continually receded from the earth. After the end of one hundred fifty days the waters decreased. The ship rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on Ararat’s […]
echoes.note: God's 'waiting patiently in the days of Noah' (3:20) reflects the long patience while the ark was built and the flood receded (Gen 8); the divine forbearance toward the disobedient generation undergirds the patience motif. Recurrence within the Noah cycle.

echoes.text: Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.”
echoes.note: 'My Spirit shall not abide in man forever... his days shall be 120 years' — the limited span of divine patience before the flood — directly informs '(God) waited patiently in the days of Noah' (3:20), the period of forbearance before judgment.

echoes.text: When men began to multiply on the surface of the ground, and daughters were born to them, God’s sons saw that men’s daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives. Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.” The Nephilim were in the earth in those days, and also after that, when God’s sons came in to men’s daughters and had children […]
echoes.note: The 'sons of God' who transgressed before the flood (Gen 6:1-4) feed the Second-Temple Watchers tradition (1 Enoch) widely thought to lie behind 'the spirits in prison' to whom Christ preached (3:19). Contested: whether the spirits are fallen angels (Watchers) or the human dead of Noah's generation.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous' (3:18) draws on the Servant who 'bore the sin of many' and 'the righteous one, my servant, shall make many to be accounted righteous.' The vicarious righteous-for-unrighteous formula extends 1 Peter's sustained use of Isaiah 53 (cf. 2:22-25).

echoes.text: The earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence. God saw the earth, and saw that it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth. God said to Noah, “I will bring an end to all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence through them. Behold, I will destroy them and the earth.
echoes.note: The 'disobedient' spirits/generation 'who before were disobedient in the days of Noah' (3:19-20) echo the corruption and violence that filled the earth (Gen 6:11-13). Faint, depends on identifying the 'spirits in prison' with the Noahic generation.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: The Servant who is 'exalted and lifted up' parallels the exaltation of the suffering-then-glorified Christ 'at the right hand of God, having gone into heaven' (3:22). Faint, part of the Isaiah 52-53 Servant arc.

echoes.text: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.
echoes.note: 'Put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit' (3:18) and Christ's descent/proclamation faintly echo the Psalm of resurrection hope ('you will not abandon my soul to Sheol'), a text early Christians applied to Christ's vindication from death. Faint, thematic.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The exaltation of the suffering one to heavenly dominion over 'angels and authorities and powers' (3:22) recalls the Son of Man given everlasting dominion and all powers subjected to him. Faint, thematic cosmic-subjection parallel.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: The heavenly voice 'You are my beloved Son' echoes the royal enthronement decree 'You are my Son' of Psalm 2:7. Volume is high (the opening clause is near-verbatim) and recurrence is strong (Mark 9:7; the title frames the Gospel). Coherence is maximal: the baptism functions as a messianic enthronement, declaring Jesus the Davidic king-son.

echoes.text: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.
echoes.note: 'In whom I am well pleased' draws on the Servant of Isaiah 42:1, 'my chosen, in whom my soul delights,' paired with the Spirit resting on him (v.10). Volume is high on the 'well pleased / delight' clause and the Spirit-endowment, and the fusion of royal Son (Ps 2) with suffering Servant (Isa 42) is a load-bearing Markan Christology. Coherence is high.

echoes.text: Oh that you would tear the heavens, that you would come down, that the mountains might quake at your presence,
echoes.note: Mark's distinctive 'the heavens being torn' (schizomenous) recalls Isaiah 64:1 LXX, 'O that you would rend the heavens and come down.' Volume rests on the violent verb 'tear,' which Mark uniquely chooses (vs. Matthew/Luke's 'opened') and reuses at the temple veil (15:38). Coherence is high: God rends the heavens to descend in the Spirit upon Jesus.

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: 'Beloved Son' (agapētos) may invoke Isaac, 'your only/beloved son,' in the Aqedah of Genesis 22:2 LXX, foreshadowing the offered son. Volume is the single distinctive adjective agapētos (which LXX uses for Isaac), giving real verbal contact; recurrence at 9:7 and the passion's sacrificial logic raise coherence. Genuinely contested—agapētos may simply intensify 'Son.'

echoes.text: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
echoes.note: The Spirit descending over the baptismal waters may evoke the Spirit/wind hovering over the primordial waters of Genesis 1:2, framing the baptism as new creation. Volume is conceptual only (no 'dove' in Genesis), so the link is faint; some rabbinic traditions compared the Genesis Spirit to a bird, which marginally supports it. Contested.

echoes.text: Now in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth of the month, as I was among the captives by the river Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's inaugural vision opens with 'the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God,' a prophetic-commission topos that Mark's heaven-rending and Spirit-descent may share. Volume is low and the verb differs (open vs. tear), so this is a generic apocalyptic-opening echo rather than a targeted citation; included for completeness.

echoes.text: Then he remembered the days of old, Moses and his people, saying, Where is he who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of his flock? where is he who put his holy Spirit in their midst? who caused his glorious arm to go at the right hand of Moses? who divided the waters before them, to make himself an everlasting name? who led them through the depths, as a horse in the wilderness, so that they didn’t stumble? As the livestock that go down into […]
echoes.note: Isaiah 63 recalls God putting his Holy Spirit among his people at the Exodus through the sea, a new-Exodus matrix coherent with Jesus' Spirit-anointing at the Jordan. The contact is thematic (Spirit + water + sonship of Israel) rather than verbal, so volume is low; it strengthens the new-Exodus reading of the whole prologue.

echoes.text: You shall remember all the way which Yahweh your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to prove you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments, or not.
echoes.note: Jesus' forty days 'tempted' in the wilderness recapitulates Israel's forty years in which the LORD led them to test (peirazō) them. Volume is thematic (forty + wilderness + testing) rather than verbal, but the typology of the new Israel re-running the wilderness probation is coherent and recurrent in early Christian reading. Mark, unlike Q, gives no scriptural debate, so the link is figural.

echoes.text: He was there with Yahweh forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread, nor drank water. He wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten commandments.
echoes.note: Moses' forty days and forty nights on Sinai (also Exodus 24:18) supplies one of the canonical 'forty days' fasts that Jesus' wilderness sojourn evokes. Volume is the shared numeral and wilderness setting; the Moses typology is coherent with Mark's broader new-Exodus framing, though Mark's brevity keeps it allusive rather than verbal.

echoes.text: He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!” He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again. Yahweh’s angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.” He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty […]
echoes.note: Elijah's forty days in the wilderness, sustained by an angel who 'served' him with food, closely parallels Mark's 'forty days... and the angels were serving him.' Volume includes the shared forty days plus angelic ministration, a distinctive combination; given Mark's heavy Elijah typology (John as Elijah, 1:6), recurrence and coherence are notable.

echoes.text: For he will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you in all your ways. They will bear you up in their hands, so that you won’t dash your foot against a stone. You will tread on the lion and cobra. You will trample the young lion and the serpent underfoot.
echoes.note: Psalm 91 promises angelic guardianship and treading on lion and serpent unharmed; Mark's pairing of 'wild animals' and 'angels serving him' may reflect this protection motif. Volume is low and indirect (the psalm is explicit in the Q temptation, not Mark), so for Mark this is a contested thematic echo rather than a citation.

echoes.text: The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the young goat; The calf, the young lion, and the fattened calf together; and a little child will lead them. The cow and the bear will graze. Their young ones will lie down together. The lion will eat straw like the ox. The nursing child will play near a cobra’s hole, and the weaned child will put his hand on the viper’s den. They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain; for […]
echoes.note: Jesus 'with the wild animals' may evoke the eschatological peace where beasts no longer harm, marking him as inaugurator of restored creation. Volume is purely thematic and the wild beasts in Mark could equally signal danger (cf. Ps 91), so the irenic-Eden reading is contested; included for the new-creation typology.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’”
echoes.note: The new-Adam reading sees Jesus, tempted by Satan yet among the beasts and served by angels, reversing Adam's failure in the garden among the animals. Volume is conceptual (Satan as tempter, the beasts, paradise restored) with no verbal borrowing, so this Adam-Christ typology is faint and contested in Mark, who never names Adam.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: 'The kingdom of God is at hand' announced as 'good news' fulfills the herald of Isaiah 52:7 who proclaims good news and says 'Your God reigns.' Volume couples the distinctive verb euangelizō with the reign of God, both present here; recurrence binds it to 1:1's euangelion. Coherence is maximal—this is Mark's thesis statement drawn from Isaiah's gospel of God's kingship.

echoes.text: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.
echoes.note: The expectation that 'the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed' supplies the apocalyptic content of Jesus' 'kingdom of God.' Volume is conceptual but the specific phrase 'kingdom of God/heaven' has its clearest Second-Temple anchor in Daniel; coherence with Mark's 'the time is fulfilled' (an apocalyptic timetable) is strong.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The everlasting dominion given to the 'one like a son of man' is the kingdom Mark's Jesus proclaims and later claims (Mark 13:26; 14:62). In 1:15 the contact is thematic—the inbreaking eternal kingdom—rather than verbal, but the recurrence of Daniel 7 across Mark gives the echo real weight here.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound; to proclaim the year of Yahweh’s favor, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn;
echoes.note: 'The time is fulfilled' resonates with Isaiah 61:2's 'the acceptable year of the LORD,' the proclamation of the eschatological jubilee by the Spirit-anointed herald (cf. Jesus' anointing at 1:10). Volume is moderate on the 'favorable/fulfilled time' motif; coherence with the gospel-of-God framing is good, though Mark does not quote it as Luke does.
echoes.lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind; to declare the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of recompence; to comfort all that mourn;

echoes.text: Your doom has come to you, inhabitant of the land: the time has come, the day is near, a day of tumult, and not of joyful shouting, on the mountains.
echoes.note: Ezekiel 7:7,12 declare 'the time has come, the day is near,' a near-formula for Mark's 'the time is fulfilled.' Volume is the shared 'the time has come' idiom, but Ezekiel's announcement is judgment, not gospel, weakening coherence; included as a faint, contested verbal parallel.

harmony.title: The Baptism of Jesus
harmony.note: John's Gospel reports it obliquely, through the Baptist's testimony — "I have seen and have testified that this is the Son of God."

harmony.title: The Temptation in the wilderness
harmony.note: Mark gives it in two verses; Matthew and Luke give the three temptations in full, though in differing order.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The waters close over Jesus, and the heavens tear open.
You are my Beloved; with you I am well pleased.
The Spirit drives him into the wilderness forty days.
We follow him into the wilderness.
The bow is set in the clouds; God remembers the covenant.
God's mercy holds us on the way.
The time is fulfilled; the kingdom has come near.
Come, let us turn and believe. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: The river still runs cold where Jesus went down, where the heavens tore and the dove came to rest.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Now the same Spirit drives us into the wilderness, into forty days of wind and stone and hunger.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
And over the wilderness the rainbow bends, the old promise that God will not let the waters win.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
The kingdom of God has come near; turn around, and believe the good news.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
So set out, all you who have been baptized, into this holy season.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Down into the water, then out to the wilderness.
Lead us in your way.
Forty days of wind and stone before us.
Lead us in your way.
The bow still bends above the storm.
Lead us in your way.
The kingdom has come near; we turn and believe.
Lead us in your way. Amen.
